newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia blasts Japan's move on national car.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia blasts Japan's move on national car.

text.p: Indonesia will proceed with its "national car" programme despite Japan's plans to seek a World Trade Organisation (WTO) ruling on the issue, State Secretary Murdiono told reporters on Monday.

"Indonesia is disappointed with Japan's attitude, which does not accomodate our interests," Murdiono said, adding that President Suharto had instructed officials to cease bilateral talks with Japan on the issue.

Suharto had called six ministers and the central bank governor to a surprise meeting on Monday after receiving reports that Japan intended to submit the national car policy to a WTO panel, Murdiono told reporters at the state palace.
A Japanese Trade Ministry official said last week that Japan will ask the WTO to create a panel to rule on Tokyo's complaint against Indonesia's car policy.
He said it will request that a panel be formed at the next meeting of the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body on April 30.
Murdiono said after the meeting that the national car programme was an effort at self-sufficiency.

"The move by Japan makes clear to us we should mobilise ourselves to leave the environment of economic dependence from other countries and struggle towards independence, not only in the national car but also in other sectors," he said.

Indonesia's national car policy gives PT Timor Putra Nasional, controlled by Suharto's youngest son Hutomo Mandala Putra, tax and tariff breaks to produce the Timor car in association with Kia Motors Corp of South Korea.
"Our disappointment is that Japan could not understand our national car programme," Murdiono said.
Along with Japan, the United States and the European Union have also complained about the programme, which they say has given Timor Putra an unfair price advantage in the car market.

Murdiono said consultation with the United States on the issue was continuing while Japan felt it was time to take the issue to the WTO panel. He said Suharto had instructed officials not to resume bilateral talks on the issue with Tokyo, which have stalled after two rounds.
Murdiono said the car programme would continue because a decision by the WTO, if it were to discuss the Japanese complaint, would not be made until 1999.
